Hi Jino, sorry for the delay. Thanks for tackling handling the PDRs in terms of iterators, this is generally a great thing for library ergonomics. I do have some requests inline however.

The `### Added` section is immediately below. It would make more sense to move these there.

Separately, the changelog is for users of the library. The git history records implementation details. Users should not be calling the `*_init()` and `*_next()` APIs directly. Rather, they should be using the iterator macros. Let's keep the descriptions here focused on how the user will use the APIs.
Hi Andrew, I've renamed the iterator macros as per your suggestion below and moved them to ### Added section
Done

While there are historically instances of typedefs in the codebase (e.g. immediately above), please don't add more without good reason. The only good reason right now is to abstract over a type for the purpose of renaming it down the track. I don't expect that's intended here.

Please audit the rest of the patch to remove the typedefs.
I've removed this typedef for struct pldm_state_effecter_pdr as it's not required anymore.
Done

Please make sure that the type name is appropriately prefixed:

https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/9f6b9b3aca29a022c597a87f445d487d8020fe51/CONTRIBUTING.md#L249-L264

Note that this also discusses using e.g. `_pdr_` or `_platform_` as part of that prefix.

Please audit the rest of the patch for such concerns and fix them as appropriate.

If you haven't already, please read the rest of `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

I've removed the typedef but the forward declaration of struct state_effecter_possible_states is required as adding <libpldm/platform.h> in pdr.h caused additional compilation errors. Please let me know alternative ways to resolve this.
Done

POSIX reserves the namespace of all types suffixed with `_t` (see the tables in section 2.2.2 ("The Name Space") of The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8, IEEE Std 1003.1-2024). Please avoid adding any further instances.

Additionaly, this is another typedef. Please name the struct, drop the typedef, and audit the rest of the patch for further instances of anonymous structs.
Thanks for letting me know about this. I have removed typedefs & _t suffixes from the structs.
Done

I think this is a mischaracterisation. This _is_ the API that users should use. If we're to be selective about what we document, _these_ macros are what need it. The documentation on the `*_init()` and `*_next()` APIs above is less of a priority precisely because they're hidden by use of these macros.

For an example of what I'd like to see, there's this:

https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/9f6b9b3aca29a022c597a87f445d487d8020fe51/include/libpldm/firmware_update.h#L2855-L2924
I've added them to changelogs and also added comment for it.
Done

It probably needs to be documented in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, but I'd like us to be consistent with the existing iterator macros, which means two things: Lower-case naming, and prefixing them as `foreach_`, followed by the type-name.
Done. Renamed both of them with lower case naming and prefixed them in foreach_ and relevant typename. Also added error code support so that the macro users can get error info.
Done

I'd rather not see more bespoke overflow testing. Can you discuss why you're not using the msgbuf APIs? I can't see a reason you should be avoiding them. They solve these problems in a way that, as a maintainer reviewing the changes, I know I don't have to worry about analysing whether you've missed any checks.
As per your suggestion, I've refactored my code to make use of msgbuf APIs.
Done
I expect we don't want this to be an error condition.
Removed this check from the code.
Done

Changes done:
1. Add macros in Changelog.md instead of function in ### Added section
2. Remove unnecessary typedefs
3. Remove _t from my structs
4. Rename macros with foreach_
5. Use msgbuf APIs
6. Remove check for comp eff count = 0
7. Add error code support
8. Now accepts void buffer instead of struct
9. Discard buffers on errors
10. Add more test cases

Hi Jino,

Thanks for the improvements. I have left quite a few comments, but we're starting to move down the tree of problems (away from architectural design concerns towards implementation design concerns) - so I want you to know I think this is heading in the right direction and to not be too worried about the volume.

Other parts of the libpldm API use the contracted form of `_iter`. I prefer we be consistent.

Can you please audit the change for other instances as well?

Note: There is an exception: Any symbols derived from names in relevant specifications should not have contractions. I ask this so it's easy to map the implementation back to the spec without having to guess at what letters someone chose to drop.
Done. Renamed all my iterator structs to _iter.
Done

We have `struct variable_field` for this - while I don't think its definition is great (should be `const void *ptr`), let's at least use what we have.

Please audit the change for other opportunities to switch to it.
Done. Used struct variable_field as suggested.
Done

Is it necessary to take a different design to e.g. the PLDM firmware update package parsing APIs? I'd like to be consistent if we can.

I feel that using `-ENODATA` as a signal to stop iteration will be error-prone, as it broadly behaves like any other error. Callers can no-longer just test whether the returned value is less than zero - they need an explicit carve-out for `-ENODATA`. It puts us down around a score of 3 by https://ozlabs.org/~rusty/index.cgi/tech/2008-03-30.html

By contrast, the firmware update package parsing APIs use a pattern of `*_init()` / `*_next()` / `*_end()` functions, where the latter two just return `bool`, and `_end()` being `const`. The way we extract the data is using the `decode_*_from_iter()`.

Please audit the rest of the patch for similar concerns.
Done. Reworked the methods to return 0 on success and other error codes on failures & also tried to align with firmware update function naming.
Done

I prefer we use `_end` as a suffix for consistency with the other iterator APIs.

Please audit the rest of the patch for similar concerns.
Done.
Done

Why are we asking callers to decompose this? I think we can improve the ergonomics. Can we please rather take a `struct pldm_state_sensor_pdr` and handle accessing the necessary members in the implementation?
Done. The APIs now accept struct instead of buffer.
Done

Must we ask for this? I feel it's a bit of a distraction for users. If we're concerned about shadowing we can prefix the name of the variable with e.g. `libpldm_` as we're already reserving that (along with `pldm_`) anyway.
Done. Removed this parameter from the macro argument list.
Done

What is `pdr`? A `std::vector<uint8_t>`? We should be passing around instances of representative types, i.e. a `struct pldm_state_sensor_pdr *`, not a raw byte representation of an object.

Expecting callers to pass a correct `std::vector<uint8_t>` is at most a 2 on the [How Do I Make This Hard to Misuse?](https://ozlabs.org/~rusty/index.cgi/tech/2008-03-30.html) scale, and probably more in the territory of [What If I Don't Actually Like My Users?](https://ozlabs.org/~rusty/index.cgi/tech/2008-04-01.html). I really prefer we make it easier to use correctly (harder to use incorrectly) than that.

Let's pass a `struct pldm_state_sensor_pdr *` directly. We'll still need the size argument as the struct contains a flexible array, but that's fine (even if it feels unusual - that's flexible arrays for you).

Hi Andrew, what should users (which is also our case btw) do if they have a std::vector<uint8_t> pdr containing PDR data? Do they need to convert it to struct pldm_state_effecter_pdr* before calling these macros? If yes, what would be the ideal way? I think our C++ codebase has guidelines to avoid reinterpret_cast. Should they use placement new or memcpy to copy data to a struct pldm_state_effecter_pdr object? (The latter seems wasteful for what should be a zero-copy operation.)
Would it be acceptable for the C API to take const void* so the type interpretation happens in the C implementation? The C++ callers would then simply pass pdr.data(), pdr.size() directly. This keeps the cast localized within the library rather than scattered across callers.

The problem I have with that is that the caller could be holding any old byte buffer, not necessarily anything that represents the PDR. Designing the API in the way you suggest doesn't prevent the caller from doing the wrong thing.

If the caller is already doing the wrong thing wrt to types then we shouldn't design _new_ APIs that continue to enable that.

If that forces the use of reinterpret_cast there then I think that's fair, it's a signal of the the approaching hazard. The API design should insulate the library implementation from that hazard via the type system.
Got it. Now instead of normal buffer, we're accepting struct pldm_state_effecter_pdr *.
Done

Not required anymore.

I don't think there's a need to distinguish between `inner_rc` and `rc` in the example. If the outer loop header errors we should never execute its body. If the inner header errors we can return directly from its test.
Done. Used single variable for error handling.

Hi Jino, I have a quite a few comments again but they're mostly implementation concerns and not design concerns.

I acknowledge that you're handling PDRs here, however, the existing APIs in this header are largely concerned with maintaining a PDR repository, rather than encoding or decoding specific PDR messages. Can we do a return check here? 

Currently the function still returns pldm_msgbuf_complete_consumed even if pldm_msgbuf_span_remaining failed - potentially masking the error.

The return check isn't required here as pldm_msgbuf accumulates errors on ctx and a failure in any operation (e.g. pldm_msgbuf_extract) poisons ctx->remaining to a negative sentinel, and then every subsequent operation returns early without touching its outputs. The final error is returned by pldm_msgbuf_complete_consumed(ctx), so no error is masked.
